report:
Summary finding
- The evidence points to a domain/style shift (not a single clear "task objective"): the B−A residual difference increases the model’s activation toward vocabulary from two recurring domains — (a) academic/professional credentials and technical words (e.g. "dissertation", "doctoral", "undergraduate", "professional", "technical", "molecular", "Innovation", "honors") and (b) culinary/restaurant language (e.g. "cooking", "Cook", "Restaurant", "kitchen", "baking", "Chef", "culinary", "baked", "oven", "Cake").
- This signal is concentrated in middle-to-late layers (roughly layers 10–25, with particularly large norms in layers ~15–25) and is strongest at early token positions (position 1 in many layers).

Why I conclude that
- The logit-lens top tokens for the highest-norm cells repeatedly show the same clusters of tokens across many layers: "dissertation/doctoral/undergraduate/Professional/technical/Innovation" and "cooking/Restaurant/Cook/culinary/kitchen/baking" appear very consistently.
- The L2-norm heatmap shows the difference is not localized to just one very early or final layer but grows through mid/late layers (peaking in the teens/twenties), and is strongest at position 1 (p1) for many layers — suggesting the difference affects how continuations begin and the early semantic framing of text.
- The mix of tokens (credentials/academic + culinary/professional) suggests a domain/style bias (more likely continuations about resumes/bios/technical descriptions and restaurant/food content), rather than a narrowly specified objective I can name confidently.

Uncertainty / limits
- The evidence does not uniquely identify a single training objective or precise behavioral goal (e.g., "fine-tuned for recipe generation" vs "upweighted professional bios"): it only shows increased activation toward those vocabulary clusters. Patchscope continuations (if available) would help confirm whether B actually produces more of those genres in practice.
- Some tokens (e.g. "polyurethane", "billionaire", "macroeconomic", "Obama") are less consistent with a single neat domain, so the difference may be a broader shift toward more “professional/technical/commerce/biography” style vocabulary rather than one narrow topic.

Verdict
- The evidence supports calling the difference a domain/style bias: Model B’s residuals (relative to A) push probability mass toward academic/professional and culinary/restaurant vocabulary, concentrated in middle-to-late layers and early token positions. It does not support naming a more specific objective beyond that.
